query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A targeted interfacial thermal treatment that promotes controlled segregation of select solute species (via optimized heating/cooling cycles) to the internal boundaries of eutectic high‐entropy alloys will enhance local bonding at lamellar colony interfaces. This in turn will blunt stress concentration sites, suppress microcrack initiation, and thereby simultaneously improve both tensile strength and room-temperature ductility relative to the unmodified lamellar microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy with dual‐phase lamellar colonies characterized by numerous internal boundaries that serve as preferential sites for microcrack initiation during room-temperature deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply a targeted interfacial thermal treatment designed to induce controlled segregation of selected solute species at the internal lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.conditions: The treatment is applied under controlled thermal cycling conditions (with optimized heating rate, peak temperature, hold time, and cooling rate) that preserve the dual-phase lamellar morphology while enabling segregation, with subsequent room-temperature tensile testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced chemical bonding and local cohesion at the internal boundaries resulting from the segregated solute layers, which reduce free energy at these interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The interfacial thermal treatment drives beneficial solute segregation at the colony boundaries. This segregation reinforces the interface by lowering interfacial energy and blunting stress concentrations, thereby delaying microcrack initiation without compromising the dual-phase scheme responsible for high strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated samples, the treated alloy is expected to exhibit both a higher tensile strength and significantly improved room-temperature ductility due to reduced microcrack nucleation.
generation.baseline: The unmodified eutectic alloy with its standard dual‐phase lamellar colonies that, while providing high strength, suffer from premature microcracking and limited ductility at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the treatment is contingent on the thermal treatment parameters being finely tuned; if the temperature or time deviates significantly, the lamellar morphology might degrade or excessive segregation could occur, potentially harming either strength or ductility.
generation.uncertainty: While the proposed mechanism is supported by interfacial engineering principles, the optimal treatment parameters (temperature, time, cooling profile) and the precise selection of solute species for segregation remain to be systematically determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical eutectic high‐entropy alloy samples. Subject one set to the targeted interfacial thermal treatment with refined thermal parameters and leave the other set untreated. Perform detailed microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM and atom probe tomography) to verify solute segregation at interfaces and then carry out standardized room-temperature tensile tests comparing strength, ductility, and microcrack initiation behavior.
measurements: Quantitative tensile strength (ultimate tensile strength and yield strength)
Microscopic examination of lamellar colony interfaces (using TEM/APT) to assess solute segregation
Fractographic analysis to evaluate microcrack density and initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated and untreated samples show no statistically significant differences in both tensile strength and room-temperature ductility, or if interfacial segregation is not observed and microcrack density remains unaltered, then the hypothesis that the targeted interfacial thermal treatment enhances both properties is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high‐entropy alloys (as in PMC4145285) used conventional casting and modest thermomechanical treatments (e.g., cold rolling) to generate dual‐phase lamellar microstructures that delivered high strength but could suffer from microcracking due to the abundance of internal boundaries. Subsequent studies (e.g., PMC5995863) shifted toward tuning the phase architecture via solutionizing and annealing treatments to modify the distribution and coherence of precipitates, which improved ductility at the expense of some strength. However, these efforts targeted the phase‐volume aspects (lamellar spacing, phase ordering) rather than directly addressing the local interface damage responsible for premature crack nucleation.
decision.unsolved: Despite varied thermo‐mechanical and microstructure‐architecture strategies, the root problem of highly vulnerable lamellar colony boundaries remains. None of the prior interventions specifically modify or reinforce the internal interfaces so as to block microcrack initiation without compromising the high strength that derives from the dual‐phase structure.
decision.lever: Implement a targeted interfacial thermal treatment designed to induce controlled segregation of selected solute species at the lamellar colony boundaries
decision.why: Because prior approaches have mainly altered bulk phase architecture or precipitate distributions without focusing on the bonding quality at interfaces. A thermal treatment that promotes beneficial segregation at internal boundaries will enhance local cohesion and blunt stress concentrations, thereby suppressing microcrack nucleation while retaining or even further increasing strength. This intervention directly addresses the microcracking unsolved by earlier processing methods and follows the trend of refining microstructure to protect critical interfaces.
